Friday. At dinner Sunaina's father Vikas announced that a match was "more or less fixed" and that the wedding would follow once her posting in Bhopal ended. Sunaina's rice went cold. "I would like to talk about this, Papa," she said. "What is there to discuss?" he replied.

Sunday. On the terrace she told her mother and her aunt that she was not refusing marriage; she wanted a say in whom and when. Her aunt said, "I will speak to your father."

Next Saturday. Sunaina asked her father to hear her for ten minutes without interrupting: two years to finish her fellowship, then she would gladly meet families. Vikas was silent a while. "Two years? Let me talk to your mother." She had no yes, but she had a maybe, and she had not shouted.

qa.q: What did Sunaina ask her father for on Saturday?
qa.a: She asked him to hear her for ten minutes without interrupting.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when her rice went cold?
qa.a: Sunaina was shocked and pinned between love for her family and her own wishes.
She talked to her mother and her aunt on the terrace, and her aunt offered to speak to her father.

qa.q: How might Vikas be seeing the situation?
qa.a: Vikas assumed the match was settled and saw little to discuss, but his "let me talk to your mother" shows he is starting to listen.

grounding: A family expects the protagonist to follow their marriage plan; she explains calmly, gathers allies and chooses how firmly to hold her ground.

"The Grewals are coming on Sunday," Yogesh said at dinner. "Their son is a doctor in Canada. It's decided."

Simran put her fork down. "Papa, nothing is decided. I haven't even met him."

"You're twenty-four. Your mother married at twenty."

"And I'm finishing my architecture license next year. I want to work first."

"Work? After marriage, you can do whatever your husband allows."

Simran's heart was pounding. She loved him. She also felt pinned to the wall.

"Papa, I'm not saying never. I'm saying not like this. I'd like to meet people myself, after I get my license."

Her mother spoke quietly. "She has worked hard, ji."

Yogesh looked at his wife, surprised. Simran's Bua, visiting from Ludhiana, added, "Let the girl finish, Yogesh. Times are different."

He was silent a long time. "Sunday they come for tea. Only tea. Nothing is fixed."

Simran breathed out. "Thank you, Papa."

qa.q: What profession did the Grewals' son have?
qa.a: He was a doctor in Canada.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Papa said it was decided?
qa.a: Simran felt pinned to the wall, her heart pounding, torn between love for her father and her own choices.

qa.q: What helped Simran hold her ground?
qa.a: She explained her view calmly, and her mother and Bua spoke up as allies, without anyone showing contempt.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt when his wife and sister spoke up?
qa.a: Yogesh was surprised and perhaps uncomfortable, realising he did not have everyone's agreement.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young woman whose father expects her to follow his marriage plan, who explains her view calmly and gathers allies while keeping respect.

passage:
I'm Kishore, the eldest son, and in our family that meant one thing: I would run Papa's hardware shop in Nashik and marry whoever Mummy chose. Nobody asked. It was just how things were.

But I wanted to teach. Physics, at a school. For two years I said nothing. I felt pinned between loving them and losing myself.

My younger sister Kashish was the first person I told. She said, "Bhaiya, you have to say it. And not by shouting."

So I did, on a Sunday, calmly. "Papa, I respect the shop. You built it from nothing. But I want to be a teacher." He went red. Mummy started crying.

Kashish spoke up: "He's good at it, Papa. He taught me all of Class 12 physics." Later Mama, Mummy's brother, sided with me too.

It took a year. Papa hired a manager. I teach at a school in Pune now. We still argue. But I never once called them backward, and I'm glad.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel during the two years of saying nothing?
qa.a: Kishore felt pinned between loving his family and losing himself.

qa.q: What helped Kishore follow his own path without contempt?
qa.a: He explained calmly and respectfully, gathered allies in Kashish and his uncle, and never looked down on his parents.

qa.q: How might Kishore's father have felt hearing his son's choice?
qa.a: Papa probably felt hurt and angry, going red, since he had always assumed his son would take over the shop.

grounding: A first-person account shows a young man whose family expects him to follow their plan for career and marriage, who explains calmly, gathers allies and holds firm without contempt.
